title: docs/derived/state/lineage.json — the declared provenance of everything this project derives
description: AUTHORED by the founder or the planner (writer null), the same class as requirements.json and removals.json. Two lists and nothing else: the SOURCES a project treats as truth, and the DERIVATIONS it makes from them. additionalProperties is FALSE at every level because this is a contract a checker reads field by field, and a key nothing reads is a declaration the author believes is in force while nothing enforces it. What the pack does with it is verify, never trust: kernel/lib/lineage.js compares each target's recorded marker against the source on disk, so a derivation that names a source is a claim with a digest behind it rather than a comment.

sources.description: Every file or endpoint this project treats as the truth something else is copied from. A source with no derivation is not an error: declaring the inventory before anything derives from it is how a founder records the decision in advance.

derivations.description: Every file or glob this project produced FROM one of those sources. An empty list with the file present is CANNOT_DETERMINE, never a pass: a lineage document that declares no derivation is a contract with nothing to check.

sourceId.description: A stable identifier a derivation and a marker both name. Kept to the characters a comment line can carry unambiguously, because the marker line `respawnpack-derived-from: <sourceId>@sha256:<hex>` is parsed out of a target file's own comment syntax.

source.description: Exactly one of `path` or `url`. A URL source cannot be digested by this pack, so every derivation from one reports CANNOT_DETERMINE naming that — recorded as an honest blind spot rather than resolved into a verdict nobody can stand behind.

kind.description: What KIND of truth this is, so a reader can tell an inventory from a template without opening it. The six are the shapes provenance actually takes across project types: an ops inventory, an infrastructure definition, a template a copy is cut from, an interface schema a client is generated from, a dataset, and a document.

path.description: Project-relative, POSIX separators, no parent traversal. A path that escapes the project is refused by the reader rather than followed.

authority.description: The one value there is. It is a required const rather than an optional flag so that declaring a source IS declaring it authoritative: a `sources` entry that meant something weaker would leave a reader guessing which entries the derivations are checked against.

id.description: The row's own identifier. It is what the check id `lineage:<id>` is spelled with, so a verdict names the derivation rather than a path that may be a glob.

target.description: The derived file, or a glob over derived files (`*` inside a segment, `**` across segments, `?` for one character). A glob checks EVERY matching file: one unmarked file in a generated tree is the whole point.

from.description: The source ids this target may legitimately be derived from. At least one, because a derivation with no declared source is a target nothing can be checked against.

how.description: How the copy was made. It changes no verdict; it is what a reader needs to know which repair to reach for when the source has moved.

neverFrom.description: The sources this target must NEVER be derived from — the range configuration cut from the template box rather than the per-range one. A marker naming one of these is FAIL, and the detail names both the source the marker claimed and the source this derivation declares.

required.description: Whether the target must exist. Absent or false, a missing target is CANNOT_DETERMINE (it may simply not have been generated here); true, it is FAIL. The default is the weaker answer on purpose: inferring that an absent file is a breach would turn every partial checkout into a red build.
